suggest a company has high-growth potential. More detail on Beauhurst’s

equity investment

• 
Some form of equity investment

announced and unannounced fundraisings 
An unannounced fundraising is an investment made into a private company that 
is completed without press coverage or a statement from the recipient company 
or funds that made the investment. These transactions are an integral part of the 
UK’s high-growth economy, accounting for around 70% of all equity transactions.

Foreword
Giles Thorley,
Chief Executive Officer 
at the Development 
Bank of Wales
The last ten years has seen an 
extraordinary increase in high-growth 
startups and scaleups across the 
UK. These fast-growth businesses, 
particularly in the tech sector, 
have driven job creation, attracted 
record levels of investment and 
created a world-class ecosystem of 
entrepreneurs.
The research conducted by Beauhurst 
and sponsored by the Development 
Bank of Wales in this report shows 
that Wales is playing an increasingly 
important role in the growth of British 
startups and scaleups. 
The numbers speak for themselves. 
Wales has 1,215 high-growth companies 
which have raised £882m since 2011. 
Technology businesses accounted for 
28% of these, and Cardiff and Swansea 
have firmly established themselves as 
two of the most exciting and dynamic 
tech clusters in the UK. This is a story of 
home-grown talent in Wales producing 
world-class businesses with significant 
valuations. 
The last 18 months have been 
challenging for everyone. I’m very 
proud of the role the Development 
Bank of Wales has played in providing 
additional loans through the COVID-19 
Wales Business Loan Scheme. This 
report demonstrates that Welsh 
high-growth businesses have shown 
remarkable resilience during the 
pandemic. In fact, 2020 was a record 
year for Welsh investment, with £129m 
raised by high-growth companies and 
19,453 new companies incorporated. 
Whilst this research examines 
investment activity in Wales since 2011, 
what I find most exciting is what this 
data tells us about the future of the 
high-growth ecosystem in Wales. 
A fifth of the high-growth companies 
in Wales have female founders. Whilst 
more needs to be done to increase 
this figure, it demonstrates the start of 
a community that is truly embracing 
gender diversity in business. 
More than a third of the funding 
rounds were first time equity deals, 
which suggests a strong base of new, 
ambitious companies aiming for rapid 
growth. The race is on to establish 
the first Welsh tech unicorn, but it 
is encouraging to see that we have 
created a pipeline of early stage, high 
potential businesses. Wales can be 
the engine room generating the next 
generation of British tech success stories. 
Of course, there is more to do and I 
hope this is just the beginning of a 
golden age for Welsh startups and 
scaleups. The Development Bank of 
Wales is working hard to stimulate 
growth in regions beyond Cardiff and 
Swansea to build momentum in other 
regions across the country. 
We are also working to encourage 
more co-investment into the Welsh 
market. We’ve seen increasing 
investment activity from firms like the 
IP Group, BGF, LDC, Wealth Club and 
crowdfunding platforms like Seedrs. 
Welsh businesses have now secured 
funding from investors in 14 different 
countries around the world. The 
Development Bank of Wales is aiming to 
diversify the market further to connect 
Welsh businesses to new investment 
firms in the UK and overseas. 
Most importantly, I think this report 
demonstrates the importance of equity 
investment for Welsh businesses. High-
growth UK companies that received 
equity investment grew turnover by 
19.6%, compared to 5.6% for companies 
that didn’t secure equity investment. 
My message to Welsh entrepreneurs is 
to find the right investor with shared 
values and goals and to use the funding 
support available to help realise 
the ambitions of your business. The 
Development Bank of Wales wants 
to hear from you and accelerate your 
growth.  
My thanks to Beauhurst and to 
everyone who has contributed to this 
report. I hope you enjoy reading it and 
recognising the potential in the Welsh 
high-growth ecosystem.  
“This is a story of home-grown talent in Wales producing world-class 
businesses with significant valuations… Wales can be the engine room 
generating the next generation of British tech success stories.”

3
During the pandemic it was driven 
home quite clearly that the devolved 
nations of the UK have their 
own governments, agendas, and 
demographics. This is as true for 
business populations as anything else: 
for all the commonalities across the 
UK there are as many idiosyncrasies. 
For this reason, looking at specific 
geographies in depth is hugely 
rewarding, so we are grateful for the 
support of the Development Bank of 
Wales (Banc Datblygu Cymru) that 
has allowed us to produce this report 
to look at the Welsh entrepreneurial 
ecosystem in depth.
Wales is currently home to nearly 
138,000 companies, 1,215 of which 
we’ve been able to identify as high-
growth, innovative and ambitious 
businesses. These businesses 
represent 3.5% of the UK’s high-growth 
population, which means that Wales 
already punches above its weight 
because it’s home to only 2.8% of the 
general business population.
These startups and scaleups are 
to be found across Wales, but with 
prominent hubs in Cardiff (spilling 
over into Caerphilly) and Swansea. 
Outside of these hubs, however, 
there’s an opportunity: in Conwy, for 
example, only 0.7% of the companies 
there are high-growth businesses. 
Indeed, Robin Millar MP for Aberconwy 
recently hosted an event with the 
Entrepreneurs’ Network convening 
experts to come up with practical 
ideas to improve the entrepreneurial 
ecosystem in Llandudno.
Despite this potential, some of it 
remains untapped: Wales is home 
to 3.5% of the UK’s high-growth 
companies, but only receives 2.5% 
of the UK’s equity investment deals. 
External investment —and in particular 
equity investment—is an important 
catalyst for growth. Businesses using 
equity investment grow faster: not only 
because it allows them to invest in 
equipment, staff and other tools, but 
because the investment often brings 
extra expertise to the table. An angel’s 
contribution to a fast growing business 
isn’t (and perhaps shouldn’t be) 
limited to their money; their advice and 
connections can often be invaluable too.
Although other parts of the UK win 
the lion’s share of investment, 2020 
was nonetheless a record year for 
investment in Wales. £129m was 
invested into Welsh startups and 
scaleups—the most in any year so far. 
This investment comes from a variety 
of sources including the Development 
Bank of Wales, crowdfunding platforms, 
IP Group and Fusion IP. A total of 210 
different funds have backed Welsh 
companies since 2011, the majority of 
which are based outside of Wales.
Clearly those investors have seen the 
opportunity that Wales and its startups 
and scaleups offer, but there’s much 
more potential to be tapped. A record 
19,453 companies were incorporated in 
Wales in 2020 (and another record 5,829 
in the first quarter of 2021). This latest 
crop of companies are more diverse 
than older companies: nearly a quarter 
have all female directors; 69% of them 
are outside Cardiff or Swansea. With 
the right support and—crucially —the 
right investment, these startups could 
scaleup and drive recovery from the 
pandemic in Wales.
Executive summary
Henry Whorwood,
Head of Research 
and Consultancy at 
Beauhurst
“Despite the potential, some of it remains untapped: Wales is home to 
3.5% of the UK’s high-growth companies, but only receives 2.5% of the 
UK’s equity investment deals. External investment —and in particular 
equity investment—is an important catalyst for growth.”

Investing in Wales
Equity finance and how companies use it
As a means of funding innovation, 
equity finance plays an essential role 
for economic development in the 
UK. Innovative companies may need 
equity finance at the very earliest stage 
of business right through to being a 
mature, even profitable, firm. Few raise 
capital only once, particularly as equity 
investment can support many different 
goals of a developing business; from 
taking on new staff and opening office 
space, to R&D projects and breaking 
into new markets. Page 6 of this report 
demonstrates the correlation between 
the turnover and headcount growth 
rates of high-growth companies in the 
UK with receiving equity investment.
 
High-potential businesses can navigate 
a wide landscape of equity sources, 
including venture capital, private equity, 
angel investors or crowdfunding. The 
very earliest stage businesses may take 
equity investment from business angels 
and angel networks as other investor 
types may not yet be willing to part with 
funds. Venture capital funds can also 
be a funding opportunity for young and 
therefore more high-risk businesses, 
while private equity firms look to 
invest in those more established. Other 
sources of finance include funds backed 
by universities, government or not-
for-profit organisations. An increasing 
number of businesses are looking for 
equity via crowdfunding, which usually 
operate online and allow more investors 
to participate on a smaller scale.
Though some may feel that equity 
investment represents a relinquishing of 
control when new shares are allocated 
to investors, there are great benefits 
of equity finance—and more than just 
the money itself. The right investor 
can provide expertise in growing a 
business from management experience 
to knowledge of the sector. Many angel 
investors have launched funds after 
exiting their own successful startups. 
Investor relationships can also offer 
access to networks of useful contacts; 
these may form further mentors or even 
become a company’s next investor. 
Equity finance from certain investors 
can also help to raise the profile of 
a young company, further aiding its 
growth. 
After the pandemic, the rapid company 
growth borne out of equity finance 
is more important than ever, driving 
employment and the economy on 
all levels, particularly in the regions 
outside well-known investment areas. 
Whilst Wales is home to 3.5% of the 
UK’s lifetime total of high-growth 
companies, only 2.5% of equity 
investment deals are secured by these 
businesses. Meanwhile, 33% of the 
high-growth companies in the UK are 
headquartered in London, yet these 
receive 48% of equity deals. Certainly 
deserving greater investment, Wales 
is an expanding ecosystem offering  a 
wide pool of innovative developing 
companies looking to secure equity 
and reap its benefits.

new shares by a company 
to fund its growth.

higher three-year compound annual growth rates (CAGRs) in turnover 
and headcount. Of the companies that had achieved the impressive 
feat of more than 100% annual growth in turnover over the last three

compared to only 5.1% for companies that had not.

8
Investing in Wales
One of the top sectors where high-
growth Welsh businesses are operating 
is Software-as-a-Service (SaaS), with 80 
currently active companies. Between 
2011 and 2020, Welsh SaaS companies 
raised £145m in equity investment 
across 217 deals—a full breakdown 
of investment across the sectors is 
on page 14 of this report. Outside 
these figures, the Welsh ecosystem 
also supports Software-as-a-Service 
businesses with satellite offices in Wales 
and headquarters elsewhere. Artificial 
Intelligence startup We Build Bots is 
based in Cardiff as well as London, and 
has secured four fundraising rounds, 
including £250k from the Development 
Bank of Wales.
Wales is also a centre for businesses 
in high-growth property/land 
development,construction, and 
associated services, with the same 
number headquartered in the 
region as SaaS businesses. Some of 
these companies will be traditional 
construction groups, others will be 
tech-driven “proptech” companies. 
Companies in the sector include 
SystemGlaze, hatch. and Urban 
Intelligence, all of which have raised 
equity investment, contributing to 
the strength of the Welsh property 
development and construction sector.
A total of 522 active high-growth 
companies fall under the umbrella of 
business and professional services, 
which includes sectors such as recruitment 
agencies, and analytics and insights.

sensitive detection of pathogens in blood when sepsis is suspected in a patient, meaning medical staff 
are more informed to act quickly. The company has been popular with investors, raising £14.8m of equity 
funding over 13 rounds from a range of sources including business angels and venture capital. Momentum’s 
crucial backer has been the Development Bank of Wales, which has provided funding through seven deals 
between 2014 and 2020. The bioscience venture has also been awarded four Innovate UK grants worth 
£1.51m to improve patients outcomes in cases of sepsis.

Cryptocurrency is rapidly catching more mainstream attention, however it remains a form of currency hugely 
targeted by hackers or easily lost by human error. Launched in 2018, fintech venture Coincover combines 
insurance and digital security technology to provide protection for digital assets. The company has already 
secured five fundraising rounds with the Development Bank of Wales as a key investor. Most recently, 
Coincover raised £5.05m from US investors Avon Ventures, CMT Digital and DRW Venture Capital in addition 
to British fund Element Ventures, demonstrating the recognition of Welsh innovation talent from overseas. 
Occurring in July 2021, this deal gave Coincover a post-money valuation of £20m.

Marine Power Systems develops technology that harvests energy from the oceans. The company offers 
multiple devices: a mechanism that converts energy from waves, floating wind turbines that can be anchored 
even in water too deep for fixed foundations, or a dual device that can do both. This marine energy technology 
is designed to be stable and high-performance, and easy to manufacture, transport, deploy and maintain. 
Marine Power Systems has secured equity investment from business angels and crowdfunding platforms, and 
most recently raised a round worth £4.12m in August 2021. The renewable energy venture has also received 
ten grants worth £9.44m from public bodies including Innovate UK and the Welsh government’s SMARTCymru.

Though based in the small former mining town of Ammanford in Carmarthenshire, Victorian Sliders is a major 
manufacturing centre of sliding sash windows and reported turnover of £18.5m in 2020. The firm has a 240,000 
sq ft factory at its headquarters with state-of-the-art equipment for extrusion, cutting, welding and glazing, in 
addition to multiple office locations around the UK. Victorian Sliders took £1.5m of loan investment in 2017 
from the Development Bank of Wales as well as £300k in 2020 from the Coronavirus Business Interruption 
Loan Scheme (CBILS). In 2021, Victorian Sliders secured its first equity funding—£14m from BGF Growth 
Capital to assist in further accelerating growth.

11
Investing in Wales
Forming around 3% of all UK exits, 106 
high-growth Welsh businesses have exited 
the ecosystem since 2011, with seven 
undergoing an IPO and 99 choosing to be 
acquired. Raising equity remains vital for 
many businesses to make the full journey 
through the high-growth ecosystem; 44% 
of the 106 exits had previously raised 
equity, and this figure rises to 61% for 
those operating in the technology sector.
Six of the seven high-growth Welsh 
businesses that underwent an IPO chose 
to list on the Alternative Investment 
Market (AIM). Based in Bridgend, building 
materials supplier Brickability raised 
£56.7m from its 2019 IPO and achieved 
the largest market capitalisation at IPO 
to date among Welsh high-growth firms 
of £150m. High-growth Welsh businesses 
have also received international interest. 
Microelectronics manufacturer SPTS 
Technologies was acquired in 2014 by 
Israeli technology company Orbotech, 
while Invertek Drives was bought by 
Japanese firm Sumitomo Heavy Industries 
in 2019.
Other high-growth companies in the 
UK have also exited with the support of 
the Welsh ecosystem. Based in both the 
Alderley Park BioHub in Cheshire and a 
lab in Denbighshire in northwest Wales, 
the growth of BiVictriX Therapeutics was 
supported by the Development Bank of 
Wales across multiple equity rounds and its 
2021 IPO. Founder and CEO Tiffany Thorn 
is now one of the youngest female CEOs of 
a UK-based publicly listed technology firm.

Investing in Wales
Over £880m of equity funding was 
invested into high-growth Welsh 
businesses in the decade between 
2011 and 2020 across more than 
1,200 deals. One of the companies 
raising large amounts of equity is 
CSC, known in full as the Compound 
Semiconductor Centre. The space 
offers access to cutting-edge facilities 
for product and skills development  
and commercialisation of 
semiconductor material technologies. 
CSC, a Cardiff University spinout, has 
raised £54.3m of equity investment 
over three rounds, including a £51.4m 
deal in 2015 which contributed to a 
distinct peak in investment activity 
that year.
While the most deals occurred in 
2017 at 157, the largest volume of 
investment took place in 2020 at 
£129m, suggesting the confidence 
of investors in innovative Welsh 
companies has remained, in spite of 
uncertainty caused by the pandemic. 
The top equity deals of 2020 are 
outlined on page 19.
More than a third of the deals over 
the 10 years were instances of 
companies raising equity for the first 
time, demonstrating that the Welsh 
ecosystem is growing all the time. With 
new innovation continually coming to 
the fore, the outlook for investment 
opportunities in Wales looks bright.

The Development Bank of Wales dominates as the biggest equity investor 
into Welsh high-growth businesses. Set up by the Welsh government, the 
Development Bank aims to boost the economy of the region by providing 
finance to high-potential ventures across a broad portfolio of equity and 
loan funds. Development Bank of Wales funds participated in 470 unique 
equity deals between 2011 and 2020, strengthening the Welsh high-
growth landscape by elevating untapped startup innovation.
Another popular method for raising capital was crowdfunding, with 
well-known platforms Seedrs and Crowdcube ahead of traditional 
private equity and venture capital firms. The majority of companies using 
crowdfunding were in the seed-stage at the time of fundraising, with the 
size of a deal averaging at £482k by mean and £280k by median. With 
other backers less willing to invest at such an early and therefore risky 
stage, crowdfunding has become an important means of fundraising.

Almost a fifth of founders of high-growth 
companies in Wales are women. Access to 
capital, grants and other funding sources 
is often disproportionately more difficult 
for female founders, meaning becoming a 
high-growth business is on average a greater 
challenge.
The high-growth Welsh ecosystem is led by 
founders of all ages, with the vast majority 
currently aged between 30 and 59, meaning 
the most likely age bracket for incorporating a 
company is 30 to 39.
Unsurprisingly due to geographical proximity, international founders are most likely to be from 
Ireland, and then other European countries. As well as Ireland, the United States and Australia 
feature on the list, likely linked to also being English speaking. In addition to those on this 
ranking, there was one founder each from Argentina, Austria, Czech Republic, Denmark, Egypt, 
Greece, Libya, Mexico, Nigeria, Norway, Singapore, Slovakia, South Africa and Zimbabwe. 
Launching innovative businesses with the ability to grow requires a 
continual influx of entrepreneurial and talented founders. Without 
them, the high-growth ecosystem would stagnate. Such business 
leaders can come from any background and their demography is 
ever-shifting. In 2021, women currently make up 19.2% of Wales’ high-
growth founders. Though women are still greatly underrepresented in 
the equity landscape, this figure represents a rising number of female 
entrepreneurs, leading companies in several sectors including business 
services, education, food and drink, mobile apps and Software-as-
a-Service. The Welsh ecosystem is also made up of founders from 
a range of age groups, with 24.5% under 40 years of age and 5.5% 
under 30. In addition, there are currently 61 entrepreneurs with a 
non-UK nationality who are founders of active high-growth businesses 
headquartered in Wales.

variety of Welsh innovation.

COVID-19 impact status over time for Welsh high-growth businesses (2020-2021)
As in every other region of the UK, 
high-growth companies in Wales were 
impacted by COVID-19. With physical 
premises forced to close, key customer 
losses and staff sent home, the pandemic 
posed a major challenge for young 
growing businesses. The most negative 
impact was felt nearest the start of 
the pandemic, with around a fifth of 
companies affected severely or critically.
Over time, high-growth companies in 
Wales have demonstrated their resilience 
and adaptability, with the number of 
businesses affected moderately or worse 
in decline, and an increasing amount in 
recovery. Indeed, 301 Welsh companies 
in the high-growth space were able to 
create job opportunities during COVID-19. 
Examples of such companies include 
sustainable packaging manufacturer 
Transcend Packaging, window glazing 
specialist Victorian Sliders, and data 
management service for gene therapy 
patients Trakcel.
A small group of companies experienced 
a surge in demand during the pandemic. 
These 82 companies operate in areas 
such as healthcare products and supplies, 
medical instrumentation, IT services, 
Software-as-a-Service and mobile apps. 
Innovating solutions to new needs, a 
few businesses launched during the 
pandemic. Based in Swansea, My Mask 
Fit incorporated in June 2020, developing 
custom-fit and reusable PPE masks. In 
October, Innovate UK granted £171k to 
support the project.

Beauhurst is a searchable database of the UK’s high-growth companies. 
Our platform is trusted by thousands of business professionals to help them 
find, research and monitor the most ambitious businesses in the UK. We collect 
data on every company that meets our unique criteria of high-growth; from 
equity-backed startups to accelerator attendees, academic spinouts and fast-
growing scaleups.
Our data is also used by journalists and researchers who seek to understand the 
high-growth economy, and powering studies by major organisations—including 
the British Business Bank, HM Treasury and Innovate UK—to help them develop 
effective policy.
For more information and a free demonstration, visit beauhurst.com
The Development Bank of Wales is here to help businesses get the capital 
they need to start up, strengthen and grow.  
Investing around £100 million per  annum, our aim is to unlock potential in 
the economy of Wales by increasing the provision of sustainable, effective 
finance in the market.
Finance up to £10 million per round is available through loans and equity 
investment  for early stage and existing businesses. We currently manage 
a range of public and private funds totalling over £1 billion.
When Welsh businesses are strong, Wales is strong.

Focused on innovation in clinical diagnostics, Momentum is developing technology to allow rapid and highly
sensitive detection of pathogens in blood when sepsis is suspected in a patient, meaning medical staff
are more informed to act quickly. The company has been popular with investors, raising £14.8m of equity
funding over 13 rounds from a range of sources including business angels and venture capital. Momentum’s
crucial backer has been the Development Bank of Wales, which has provided funding through seven deals
between 2014 and 2020. The bioscience venture has also been awarded four Innovate UK grants worth
£1.51m to improve patients outcomes in cases of sepsis.

Cryptocurrency is rapidly catching more mainstream attention, however it remains a form of currency hugely
targeted by hackers or easily lost by human error. Launched in 2018, fintech venture Coincover combines
insurance and digital security technology to provide protection for digital assets. The company has already
secured five fundraising rounds with the Development Bank of Wales as a key investor. Most recently,
Coincover raised £5.05m from US investors Avon Ventures, CMT Digital and DRW Venture Capital in addition
to British fund Element Ventures, demonstrating the recognition of Welsh innovation talent from overseas.
Occurring in July 2021, this deal gave Coincover a post-money valuation of £20m.

Sector Clean energy generation
Incorporation date August 2008
Headquarters Swansea
Total funding raised £9.13m
Headcount (FYE 2020) 12
Marine Power Systems develops technology that harvests energy from the oceans. The company offers
multiple devices: a mechanism that converts energy from waves, floating wind turbines that can be anchored
even in water too deep for fixed foundations, or a dual device that can do both. This marine energy technology
is designed to be stable and high-performance, and easy to manufacture, transport, deploy and maintain.
Marine Power Systems has secured equity investment from business angels and crowdfunding platforms, and
most recently raised a round worth £4.12m in August 2021. The renewable energy venture has also received
ten grants worth £9.44m from public bodies including Innovate UK and the Welsh government’s SMARTCymru.
Sector Specialist window manufacturer
Incorporation date December 2005
Headquarters Carmarthenshire
Total funding raised £14.0m
Headcount (FYE 2020) 186
Though based in the small former mining town of Ammanford in Carmarthenshire, Victorian Sliders is a major
manufacturing centre of sliding sash windows and reported turnover of £18.5m in 2020. The firm has a 240,000
sq ft factory at its headquarters with state-of-the-art equipment for extrusion, cutting, welding and glazing, in
addition to multiple office locations around the UK. Victorian Sliders took £1.5m of loan investment in 2017
from the Development Bank of Wales as well as £300k in 2020 from the Coronavirus Business Interruption
Loan Scheme (CBILS). In 2021, Victorian Sliders secured its first equity funding—£14m from BGF Growth
Capital to assist in further accelerating growth.
